component.name: Shizumu
component.summary: A private writing app to think in

description.p: Shizumu is a private writing app. Open it and start the sentence: there is nothing to structure first, and nowhere to file it. You write to think, you pin what matters, and you trail what continues. The volume of writing is not the artifact; what you pin is. Every page starts empty, so the first sentence is the first thing that happens.

Pages flow into a daily memory you can scroll back through and search by content. Pins lift the lines that matter out of the daily stream: checklists, references, anything you want close at hand. Trails group writing that belongs together (a project, a book, an ongoing thread of thought) without forcing you to design a structure first, and the first time you put a page on a trail, the pins you already kept there come back onto the page. A trail can be a run of dated pages, or a continuous trail: one living document for a thread that should keep growing, such as a book, with a marker for each day you wrote in it. That is the one intentional exception, and you choose it.

The editor is keyboard driven. Type / for a table, a chart, an outline or a block of code; type @ to reach a page, a pin or a trail. Ctrl+K opens the trail index, Ctrl+P pins from the cursor, Ctrl+F finds, and a shortcuts panel lists the rest.

Local-first by design. Everything stays on your device, in a SQLite database you can open with any compatible tool. Sync is optional and end-to-end encrypted: your writing is sealed on your device before it leaves it, the keys are derived there and never leave, and the relay holds what it cannot read. Neither can we. Your writing remains yours.

Shizumu fits the writer who keeps a daily log, the developer with one trail per project, the student capturing reading notes, and anyone who wants a private place to write to think without learning a system first.

Shizumu est une application d'écriture privée. Ouvrez-la et commencez la phrase : rien à structurer d'abord, nulle part où classer. Vous écrivez pour penser, vous épinglez ce qui compte, vous suivez ce qui continue. Le volume d'écriture n'est pas l'objet ; ce que vous épinglez l'est. Chaque page commence vide, alors la première phrase est la première chose qui arrive.

Les pages s'écoulent dans une mémoire quotidienne que vous pouvez parcourir et rechercher par contenu. Les épingles soulèvent les lignes qui comptent hors du flux : listes, références, tout ce que vous voulez garder à portée. Les pistes regroupent les écrits qui vont ensemble (un projet, un livre, un fil de pensée en cours) sans imposer de structure préalable, et la première fois qu'une page rejoint une piste, les épingles que vous y aviez gardées reviennent sur la page. Une piste peut être une suite de pages datées, ou une piste continue : un seul document vivant pour un fil qui doit continuer à grandir, comme un livre, avec un repère pour chaque jour d'écriture. C'est l'exception intentionnelle, et vous la choisissez.

L'éditeur se pilote au clavier. Tapez / pour un tableau, un graphique, un plan ou un bloc de code ; tapez @ pour atteindre une page, une épingle ou une piste. Ctrl+K ouvre l'index des pistes, Ctrl+P épingle depuis le curseur, Ctrl+F recherche, et un panneau de raccourcis liste le reste.

Local d'abord, par conception. Tout reste sur votre appareil, dans une base SQLite que vous pouvez ouvrir avec n'importe quel outil compatible. La synchronisation est optionnelle et chiffrée de bout en bout : vos écrits sont scellés sur votre appareil avant d'en sortir, les clés y sont dérivées et n'en sortent jamais, et le relais ne détient que ce qu'il ne peut pas lire. Nous non plus. Vos écrits vous appartiennent.

Shizumu convient à l'auteur qui tient un journal, au développeur avec une piste par projet, à l'étudiant qui prend des notes de lecture, et à quiconque cherche un endroit privé pour penser en écrivant, sans devoir apprendre un système d'abord.

description.p: A pin holds the whole passage. Select several blocks and pin them, and the pin keeps every one of them, in order, after an edit, after a restart and on your other device. Before, the pin came out with only the first block in it. Editing a pin of several blocks replaces each block on the page once, with nothing left over, and choosing a trail for a new page brings such a pin onto it whole. If part of a selection is already pinned, the app says so instead of offering a pin button that does nothing.

The desktop looks like the phone. The page sits on the desk as a sheet with a visible edge in cream, white and dark. Text that should step back uses a quieter colour instead of fading, and every screen was measured for contrast in all three tones. The page dots are crisp, with the current page as a small pill in the accent colour. Pin and modal titles rename in place, keyboard focus shows the same ring everywhere, and the interface labels use the phone's typeface.

On the phone, @ mentions a page, a pin or a new trail, and backlinks list the pages that mention them. Deleting a page from the pages of the day asks first. Ticking a task no longer jumps the page to its end, editing a pin no longer adds an empty line to it, and a table's last cell can be tapped again.

A trail can be renamed or deleted from where you look at it: the trail sheet on the phone, and ctrl+k on the desktop. Deleting a trail keeps its pages, without a trail, and trails inside it move up with their pins.

Pairing a device to an account that is already full no longer leaves the new device half set up. Its keys are saved only once pairing completes, it waits between retries, and the message says the account is full.

Smaller fixes: mentions follow a page renamed or deleted on the other device, backlinks include pages written on the other device, screen readers hear the desktop's notices and every icon button is named, reduced motion stills every animation, scrolling in a modal stops at its edge, and Android builds use 16 KB memory pages.

A new layout for phones. On a phone, shizumu now opens on a page built for a thumb and a keyboard instead of the desktop window squeezed down. The header carries the day, the trail, how many pins the page keeps, and find. While you type, one strip sits above the keyboard and follows the caret: insert comes first and opens the slash menu as a sheet you can search by name. The block the caret is in gets a handle in the margin, and a long press on it lifts the block so you can drag it somewhere else. Tables are sized with a thumb and the chart builder works on a small screen. Sheets open at the size of what they hold and close with a flick.

The rest of the app came with it. Pins have their own screen: tap one to read it, edit it in place, or move it to another trail, and the edit is written into the block it was pinned from. Memory searches, filters by date from a month calendar, and scopes to a trail from a sheet. A trail can start inside another one, a living document can be started and reached from the phone, and a trail can be renamed, moved or deleted from memory. Sync is set up, paired by camera, switched on and off and disconnected from the phone itself. A page that cannot take writing, such as a past day, says why instead of staying silent. Tapping an attachment on Android opens it in an app that can show it, rather than offering to send it somewhere. The date on a living document opens a list of its days, and picking one takes you there.

Sync is much more dependable between two devices. A sentence typed a moment before the other device's changes arrived could disappear from the screen and from the database; it now stays. Leaving a page whose writing had not arrived yet no longer saves the empty copy over the other device's words. A page deleted on one device is deleted on the others, and one deleted on one device but still being written on the other is kept on both. Writing that arrives from another device can be found by search again. A living document written on one device is readable on the other. Memory, the pins list and an open page show what the other device wrote without being reopened, and an image whose file arrives a little after its page is drawn when it lands. A device that joins an account starts from the newest snapshot instead of replaying every change, and a device that starts over or moves to a new account no longer brings back trails, pages or pins that were deleted, and no longer fails with "no content key".

The lock setting does what its row says. With the lock on, you can now change its passphrase or turn it off again, and lock after inactivity opens and takes effect without a restart. When the app locks itself after a while, an encrypted database is closed behind the lock screen until the right passphrase opens it again. The setup screen shows whole, no longer clipped inside a box with its encrypt button hidden, and it has a cancel button. Backups of an encrypted database work and keep their passphrase. A database that will not open shows a screen saying so, with its path, instead of the app closing.

Pins and mentions. An @-mention of a pin no longer overwrites that pin: saving the page that mentioned it used to replace the pin's content with the mention and move the pin there. A mention of a pin on another trail opens that pin. An edit made to a pin from memory or the pins panel is written into its block, so the page's next save no longer undoes it on every device, and an edit that has nowhere to go is said rather than dropped. Pressing pin on a block that is already pinned says so instead of making a second pin. While all trails are showing, the pins in memory are grouped by trail.

Trails. Deleting or folding a nested trail moves its children up to the same place on every device, where before each device could end up with a different tree. The trail picker keeps those children where they belong instead of offering to create them again. Delete all writing now also removes attachments and their files, as the setting says it does.

On the desktop. The interface type is finally set in DM Mono and italics in Lora: the font files that shipped had almost no Latin letters in them, so every platform had been drawing a substitute, and there were no bold faces at all. Copied text pastes into other apps as you wrote it, without stray backslashes. Search in memory finds older writing, not only the last hundred pages, and lists every match newest first. A page holding only its focus line can be found by it. Escape inside a block no longer throws the caret to the end of the page, and closing find clears its highlights and gives the caret back. Past eight pages in a day, the page dots become a count, and a page can still be deleted from there. A pasted image with no file extension is inserted, and so is a screenshot pasted on Linux, which used to make nothing at all. An @ or a / typed inside code stays as typed instead of opening a menu. Ctrl+Left and Ctrl+Right move the caret by a word while you write instead of turning the page; Ctrl+Page Up and Ctrl+Page Down turn it from anywhere. When a save fails, one line on the page says so and the app keeps trying.

Two fixes from the issue tracker. A title you give a pin now stays on it. Pinning a sentence, naming it, and finding the name gone was the common case: the name was saved and then overwritten a moment later by the page's own save, and only pins made from a list, an outline, a table or another shaped block were spared. Renaming a pin afterwards holds too.

An outline nested inside another outline is now drawn as one. Typing the quote marker on a line already inside an outline did nest it, but the result was indistinguishable from the line before it, so the keystrokes looked as though they had been swallowed. Nested outlines already in your pages become visible with this release. Nothing was lost and nothing is created.

Fixes the Flatpak build. The 0.7.6 tree referenced an image from a directory the public source mirror does not ship, so the Flathub build could not resolve it. Nothing else changed: 0.7.7 is 0.7.6 plus that fix, and everything described below arrives with it.

New shapes for a page. A decision block records what you considered, what you chose, and why. Any block can now turn into another from the chip on its edge: a list becomes an outline, an outline becomes question and answer, any of them become plain paragraphs. The text survives, the shape changes. A convert refuses rather than guesses, so a block holding a diagram or a table will not flatten it away.

Tables ask for their size when you make them instead of always arriving three by three, and the chart builder draws while you type instead of after you save. Tables and charts are ordinary blocks now: they carry a title, and their chip opens the same actions every other block has. Before this, tapping the chip on an empty chart or table did nothing at all.

A pinned image shows the picture rather than a file row, and an image line offers pin and copy on hover, having been read as a blank line until now. An empty block is no longer pinnable. Search finds block titles. No blank line is parked above the first block on a page, and a new block lands on its own line instead of swallowing the sentence you had just written.
The client is now licensed Apache-2.0. The sync relay remains AGPL-3.0.

Fixes the snapshot upload that 0.7.4 introduced. Devices were preparing a snapshot of the account and the relay was refusing it, so a device joining had nothing to start from and fell back to replaying the whole history one change at a time. The upload now follows the order the relay expects, and the one-step first sync works as described.

Recovery works on the hosted relay. Type your 24-word phrase on a fresh install and the account it belongs to comes back. Before this, a known phrase was refused as already registered, with nothing to do next.

A new device syncs in one step. Every device publishes a snapshot of the account as it goes; a device joining takes the newest one and pulls only what came after, instead of replaying every change since the account began, one request at a time. Ops for one batch are now fetched six at a time as well.
Tapping into and out of an empty focus line no longer clears the title on your other device. The rail numbers pages by their order, so the same page has the same number everywhere.
The device list shows when each device was last heard from and explains that reinstalling the app creates a new device, so the old one can be revoked before the two-device tier fills up.

Sync correctness. A page arriving on your second device now keeps its focus line and its trail: each field carries its own timestamp, so a newer edit to one field no longer discards an older edit to a different one. That failure was not cosmetic, because a page with no focus line and no trail looked empty to the tidy-up pass and was deleted.

The two sides of that tidy-up now agree on what empty means. A page holding a focus line or belonging to a trail is never garbage, and one device can no longer delete a page another device considers worth keeping.
Pages are addressed by their own identifier rather than by a per-device number, so reopening the page you were last on takes you to that page on every device.
On Android, export and database backup work. Both previously failed with an invalid path error; they now hand the file to the system share sheet.

Packaging and links. The Flatpak build now embeds the app's interface rather than looking for a development server that is not there, and the sandbox is allowed to reach the network, so sync works when installed that way. Bug reports point at the issue tracker on the public repository.

Open beta, and sync arrives. Your writing syncs between your devices end to end encrypted, and the relay that passes it never holds your keys, so it only ever sees ciphertext. Run that relay on your own server, free and unlimited under the AGPL, or use the hosted one: two devices and a gigabyte of attachments, permanently free. Writing itself is never metered on any tier.
Android and Windows join Linux as first builds. Both are honestly labelled: beta means rough edges remain, and it means we would like you to find them.

Both spaces are quieter. Less chrome across the page and memory, and a long pass through the accumulated bug list: the editor settles, the Windows installer settles, and the phone stops putting its controls on top of the words. On a phone the block toolbar keeps the keyboard up when you use it, so pinning a line no longer takes several attempts.

Pinning works on a fresh install. A first-launch database bug dropped a column the pin queries needed, so the pin button did nothing until the app was relaunched. Injecting a pin now carries its title into the block and stays live, so editing the injected copy edits the pin. A synced attachment shows its real name on other devices instead of a content hash. "what settled" keeps its label when tapped, the block controls are smaller on a phone, and a collapsed image can be reopened.

Turning on sync is one tap. The hosted relay is offered by default and says where your writing goes; running your own is still a choice away, and the writing is encrypted before it leaves the device either way.

An image that cannot load no longer leaves its controls floating over the text beneath it. The file is reported as not on this device instead, which is the honest answer. On a phone the image's sync and remove buttons are visible at rest rather than needing a hover that touch does not have.

Phone fixes. The slash and mention menus fit the screen they are on rather than opening under the status bar with their tails off-screen. An edge swipe moves between pages and no longer creates one — on a single-page day every right swipe used to make a new page. Tapping "what settled" shows what the field is instead of a bare cursor. The app no longer draws under the system bars, so the header is not printed beneath the clock. Overlays inside the editor — the chart builder, the pin prompt — land in the viewport again. Rotating to landscape no longer reads as a keyboard that never closes.

Attachments. A file you attach now syncs between your devices, up to 100 MB where the practical limit used to be about one. The bytes travel alongside the sync log instead of inside it, which is also what makes them removable: turn an attachment's sync off and the copy on the relay goes with it, rather than staying there forever. Files are sealed under your current key, so revoking a device stops it reading attachments added afterwards. A pinned file now survives the page it came from — freeing up space no longer takes it away, and unpinning is what releases the bytes. A pin whose file is not on this device says so instead of doing nothing.

The phone interface is reworked. Block actions no longer cover the block they belong to, the header stops printing today twice, and the shell fits the screen with the keyboard up instead of scrolling itself out of view. Edge swipes move between pages the way the arrow keys do on desktop. Rotating the phone keeps the phone layout rather than falling back to the desktop one. Images and files render as blocks you can resize, preview and collapse, and a pinned image looks like an image rather than a file chip.

Sync. End-to-end encrypted sync between your devices, through a relay you run yourself. A new device joins through a short pairing code; old devices can be revoked. Continuous trails ride on a CRDT (Yjs) so two devices writing into the same trail at the same time converge without losing characters or fighting cursors. Discrete pages travel under HLC ordering. Doc identifiers are encrypted in transit — the relay routes ops without learning which page they belong to. Your recovery phrase and the keys derived from it live in the system keyring (libsecret or kwallet), not in the database, so home-directory access doesn't hand over your sync identity. Settings gain a sync section with pause, resume, force-pull, device list, and op log stats. The engine can be turned off entirely if you prefer to stay fully local. The verbs hold: write, pin, trail — now across your devices.

Editor polish. Block toolbar reappears on empty boards. Frame titles render reliably. Copy works inside structured blocks. Escape behavior is unified across block types. Markdown paste preserves list and task markers across the round-trip. No surface changes; just less friction while writing.

Tray polish. Close-to-tray now keeps the app alive in the system tray instead of quitting, with a settings toggle to flip the behavior. Tray icon is redrawn at the right bit depth so it stops appearing as a colorless square on some Linux desktops.

shizumu, made flexible. Trails you've already made can be reshaped without touching the writing inside them. Rename, move under another trail, fold into a parent, or delete. A new export sends any trail (or every trail) out as readable markdown, one folder per lineage, so your words are never trapped in the app. Underneath: the block and pin rewrite (pin sync moved to a Rust-side cache hook, same-page edits propagate within one editor frame), unified Alt-arrow movement across blocks and list items, midnight transition handling so the day you wrote on stays the day you wrote on, and a quieter writing surface from the rail-system and list-marker rewrites that landed across the v0.2.x line. The verbs hold: write, pin, trail.

Stabilization release. Pin reactivity fixes: clicking a pinned item in the panel now scrolls and highlights the corresponding block in the editor; renaming a block updates the pin card label without a reload; editing a pin after moving it to a parent page now reflects in the parent's injected copy. Trail highlight updates the moment "what matters now" is saved, no nav roundtrip. Titled boards (lists, blockquotes) survive Enter on an empty item instead of disappearing. Nested outlines render as a continuation of the parent item rather than as a separate panel inside it. New keyboard tools for blocks: Alt+Up and Alt+Down move the current block past its sibling; Tab and Shift+Tab at the start of a block nest or unnest it under the previous sibling. Slash menu adds matching entries for move up, move down, nest, unnest.

Listing polish. Sharpened description (mentions search and optional end-to-end encryption), expanded keywords for note-taking discovery (notetaking, diary, daily, writer, thoughts, ideas, encrypted, minimal), and a clearer "who this is for" paragraph. No app-behavior changes.

Picker-attach replaces the page. When you pick a continuous trail from an empty scratchpad, the scratchpad is consumed instead of lingering as an extra dot. If you'd typed a focus prompt before picking, that focus carries over to today's day-marker on the trail.

Same-day reopen fix. Closing and reopening the app on the same day no longer drops continuous trails you assigned but didn't write on yet. Today's day-marker is now preserved across boots; only past-day empty markers get cleaned up. The user's active session persists; cross-day cleanup still happens naturally tomorrow.

Rail system rewrite. Continuous trails now appear on today's rail by writing on them, the WhatMattersNow gate no longer blocks the editor, and the rail orders dots by when each one was first touched today (a trail picked first sits to the left of pages created later). Empty per-day markers from days the user assigned a trail but never wrote get cleaned up on next launch, so a "I just wanted to peek at this trail" doesn't leave a phantom day-entry tomorrow. Plus several cumulative reliability fixes from rounds 2-7: keyboard-arrow page-creation, picker-attach data-loss protection, today-orphan boot sweep.

Continuous-trail rail fixes. Pressing the right arrow on a continuous trail's living doc no longer spawns empty today-pages on every press, and the desktop-icon launch on Flathub installs is fixed (the exporter was rewriting the launcher to force x11, which has no socket on Wayland sessions). Use "+" to add a new focus; the arrow walks existing rail dots.

Continuous-trail data-loss fix. Switching trails via the picker, unlinking, or moving to a discrete trail while on a continuous trail's living doc no longer destroys the source trail's history. The picker now navigates between continuous trails without merging, and refuses unsafe moves with a hint.

Continuous-trail navigation fixes. Attaching today's page to an existing continuous trail now lands you on today's section with the "what matters now" gate on the new day's first open (previously the editor opened scrolled to yesterday's content), and the prev/next arrows walk today's focuses correctly when the canonical sits on the rail (the canonical now anchors at the right edge so left-arrow no longer dead-ends).

Continuous-trail fix. Attaching today's page to an existing continuous trail now lands you on today's section, with the "what matters now" gate showing on the new day's first open. Previously the editor opened scrolled to yesterday's content.

Listing polish. Refreshed app icon (denser ripple field), correct primary brand colors, capitalized launcher entry, and a refreshed summary. Bundled the new flathub-ready screenshots highlighting v0.2 features (memory, pins panel, trail nesting, settings).

Pin and font fixes. Pinned blocks containing inline images or links no longer render empty when reopened, and opening a pin without editing no longer overwrites its stored content. The font and size selector now applies consistently across the page, the focus rail, and the pin editor.

Tighter writing canvas. The page column no longer feels narrow at small font sizes (820px floor), and the focus pill and footer hug the viewport more closely so the surface feels less stretched on a wide window.
Fix release that brings the editor source in sync with the v0.2.x feature drop. Slash commands, @ subtrails, and list shortcuts now work in the rpm/deb installs as they always have in development.
Diagnostic build to confirm list-item commands are registering correctly. Removed an unused legacy editor extension.
Fixed slash commands and the @ mention popup not opening on the deb/rpm install. Two editor extensions were colliding on the same internal plugin key in production builds; both now register cleanly.

Diagnostic build with developer tools and runtime logging enabled, helping investigate keyboard-shortcut handling on the deb/rpm install. End users will see the same app; logs are written to stderr only when launched from a terminal.

Fixed a typing-hang on KDE Plasma 6 Wayland for the deb/rpm install. The desktop launcher now routes the app through Xwayland so keyboard input reaches the writing surface reliably. Flatpak installs were unaffected.

Mixed list nesting. Bullets, numbered, and tasks freely interleave. Type @ to spawn a child trail without leaving the page. Live font family and size controls. Refreshed app icon. Polish across pins and the writing surface. Now on Flathub.
First Flathub release. Earlier installations are migrated automatically on launch.
New app icon across the window, tray, launcher and dock.
Flatpak packaging fixes and cleaner integration with KDE and GNOME tray icons.
Embed local images in the editor with resize and collapse-to-chip. Pins now follow their source page across trail moves and survive trail deletion.
Trails, pins, and the choice between continuous and discrete writing modes.
Initial release. The writing page and chronological memory view.
